intro: A woman in Mississippi lives with far less pain after doctors edit a gene in her own blood cells. A teenager meets her counselor on a video call. An older man in a Chicago park practices tai chi to keep his balance. Each of these scenes shows medicine changing, and each raises questions about safety, fairness and evidence.

In this final unit you will look at the frontiers of health care: mRNA vaccines, gene editing, personalized medicine, artificial intelligence, telehealth, antibiotic resistance and an aging world. You will also meet the people who do this work, from EMTs and nurses to researchers and licensed acupuncturists, and learn what each path needs.

Then you will do what good health workers do. You will choose a health question, find reliable sources, weigh evidence from Western and traditional perspectives fairly, and present what is known, what is not, and what you conclude. By the end you will be able to judge a health claim yourself and explain your reasons with respect.
bigQuestion: How can we use new medical knowledge wisely and fairly, and how do we know what really works?

timeline.t: James Lind compares treatments for scurvy aboard HMS Salisbury, an early controlled trial
Alexander Fleming warns in his Nobel lecture that misusing penicillin can breed resistant bacteria
The Cochrane Collaboration is founded to publish systematic reviews of health evidence
The FDA approves trastuzumab for HER2-positive breast cancer, an early targeted treatment
The Human Genome Project finishes reading nearly all of human DNA
Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier show CRISPR can be used to edit DNA
The FDA authorizes AI software to screen for diabetic eye disease; He Jiankui's edited twins spark alarm
Victoria Gray becomes the first U.S. patient treated for sickle cell disease with CRISPR-edited cells
The COVID-19 pandemic moves many visits to telehealth; the first mRNA vaccines are given
Karikó and Weissman win the Nobel Prize for mRNA work; the FDA approves a CRISPR sickle cell treatment

words.d: a vaccine that gives cells short-lived instructions to make one harmless germ protein
a gene-editing system that cuts DNA at a spot chosen by a guide RNA
changing eggs, sperm or embryos so the change can pass to future generations
choosing care based on a person's genes, tests and illness features
unfair errors in a computer program, often from training data that leaves groups out
health care delivered at a distance by video, phone or messages
the ability of bacteria to survive drugs that used to kill them
official permission from a state to work in a health profession
a study that assigns people by chance to a treatment or a comparison group
a careful summary that gathers and judges all good studies on one question
a look-alike treatment with no active ingredient, used for comparison
a reason, such as profit, that might lead someone to favor a result

test.q: Why does an mRNA vaccine not change a person's DNA?
choices: Its instructions stay outside the nucleus and break down within days
test.why: The mRNA is a short-lived instruction that does not enter the nucleus or change DNA.

choices: Somatic CRISPR editing of her own blood-forming cells
test.why: Her own stem cells were edited with CRISPR and returned; the change is not passed to children.

test.q: What is the main ethical worry about germline editing?
choices: Changes can pass to future people who cannot consent, with unknown risks
test.why: Germline changes are inherited, and future people cannot consent to unknown risks.

test.q: Trastuzumab helps tumors with extra HER2 but not others. This is an example of what?
test.why: Using a tumor's features to choose a drug is personalized, or precision, medicine.

test.q: An AI tool trained mostly on one group makes more errors with others. What is this called?
test.why: Algorithmic bias comes from training data that leaves some groups out.

test.q: Which is a real limit of telehealth?
choices: A doctor cannot do a hands-on exam through a screen
test.why: Some problems need listening or pressing on the body, which a screen cannot do.

test.q: Which habit helps keep antibiotics working?
choices: Taking antibiotics only when prescribed and exactly as directed
test.why: This is antibiotic stewardship, which slows the rise of resistance.

test.q: According to the WHO, about how many people worldwide were 60 or older in 2020?
test.why: The WHO estimate is about 1 billion in 2020, rising to about 2.1 billion by 2050.

test.q: Which career path needs college, medical school and residency?
test.why: Physicians finish college, four years of medical school and three to seven years of residency.

test.q: Which capstone question is focused enough to study?
choices: Are old remedies better than new ones?
Does tai chi reduce falls in adults over 65?
test.why: It names a population, an intervention and an outcome, so evidence can answer it.

test.q: Why is a randomized controlled trial stronger than an anecdote?
choices: Chance assignment makes groups alike, so the treatment's effect can be separated from other causes
It tells a more moving story
test.why: Random assignment and comparison separate the treatment's effect from time, chance and expectation.

test.q: A study praising an herb was paid for by the herb's seller. What should a careful reader notice?
test.why: Funding from a seller is a conflict of interest that readers should notice.

test.q: How should a capstone describe tai chi fairly?
choices: Say what the tradition teaches about qi, and report that trials suggest fewer falls
test.why: Fair writing names the tradition's ideas in its own terms and reports what trials measured.

test.q: What helped cut deaths of children under five by more than half since 1990?
choices: Many tested steps, such as vaccines, ORS, bed nets and clean water
test.why: The lesson credits many tested public-health steps working together.

test.q: Which ending best fits a health presentation?
choices: This is not medical advice; talk with a doctor, nurse or pharmacist and mention any herbs
test.why: A respectful presentation reminds listeners it is not medical advice and points them to a professional.

write.prompt: Choose one health question from this unit, such as whether tai chi prevents falls or whether new gene treatments should be widely covered. Using two or three facts or sources from the unit, state what is known, what is not known, and what you conclude, and explain why.
tips: Name each source: who, what and when.
Describe traditional practices in their own terms, then report the evidence plainly.
Match your words to the strength of the evidence: "may help" or "clearly helps."
Give the main views fairly if the question is contested.
Use the unit's terms, such as systematic review, placebo or germline.
